01 — Logo System

The mark.

The First Serve mark works across light, dark, and color contexts. Always use one of the approved logo files below — never recreate or retype it. The mark is the most consistent thing across every piece of communication; protect it.

Primary · Light Background
Reverse · Dark Background
On Ace Yellow
On Clay
On Cream
Clear Space Logo

Clear space & sizing.

Always leave breathing room around the mark. Other elements — text, photos, edges — should never enter the clear-space zone.

Minimum Clear Space
The height of the "F" in "First", on all four sides.
Minimum Size — Print
1 inch (25 mm) wide.
Minimum Size — Digital
120 px wide at any standard screen resolution.
File Formats
SVG or PNG (transparent) for digital. EPS or PDF for print. Use the master files only.
Logo · Don'ts

What not to do.

✕
Do not stretch or distort the proportions.
✕
Do not place on unapproved colors or recolor the mark.
✕
Do not place over busy backgrounds without a solid panel.
✕
Do not rotate, add drop shadows, or apply outlines.

The 60 / 30 / 10 Rule

Cream 60%Navy 30%Yellow 10%

Cream dominates as background. Court Navy carries structure and type. Ace Yellow appears only as a deliberate accent. This proportion is the strongest signal of the brand.

Pairing Rules

Navy + Yellow is the hero pairing. Clay always pairs with Cream or Navy — never directly adjacent to Yellow. Net Gray bridges anything that needs softening.

Accessibility

Navy on Cream and Cream on Navy both pass WCAG AA. Ace Yellow does not have enough contrast for text on Cream — use Yellow only with Navy or Baseline behind any text.

04 — Photography Direction

The image.

Photography should feel like a real evening at the club, not a stock shoot. Real members, natural light, candid moments. Faces and footwork carry the brand more than empty courts ever can.

01

People first.

Members mid-swing, doubles partners at the changeover, coaches with juniors. The sport is the backdrop; the people are the subject.

02

Golden hours.

Late afternoon and early evening light outdoors. Avoid harsh overhead sun.

03

Honest framing.

Wide enough to show context. Court lines and the net are good anchors.

04

Real members, with permission.

Never stock photography. Always ask before using a member's likeness, and always tag them when posting.

05

Detail shots count.

Macro shots of balls, paddles, racquets, court surfaces. Texture builds the brand quietly between hero images.

05 — Voice Pillars

The voice.

Four traits that should be present in every piece of written communication — captions, emails, signage, replies. Not a script — a tuning fork.

01

Warm

Talk like a neighbor. First names where possible. Skip formal salutations.

02

Knowledgeable

Use real racquet-sport vocabulary. Explain terms when they need it — don't dumb them down.

03

Playful

A pun, a wink, a light reference. Sparingly. Never at a member's expense.

04

Direct

Short sentences. Real information. No filler. People came here to play, not to read.

06 — Layout Templates

In the feed.

Three reusable square layouts for Instagram and Facebook posts. Each defines element placement, not specific content. The yellow circle, clay bar, and yellow background are the recognizable visual signatures — readers should be able to tell a First Serve post from across a feed.

Template C · Community Moment

Posting Rules

Cadence — aim for three feed posts per week: one announcement, one event, one community moment.
Stories daily — court conditions, weather, real-time openings. Stories beat polished feed posts for member engagement.
Logo placement — bottom edge of every post, no exceptions. Use the white logo on dark backgrounds and the black logo on Cream or Ace Yellow.
Hashtags — three to six per post. Never more. Never the same set on every post.
Captions — the first line earns the click. Lead with the news, not the brand name.
Replies — respond to the first comment within sixty minutes whenever possible. That responsiveness is the brand.
Tag generously — members (with permission), partners, sponsors, USTA leagues. Algorithms reward it; relationships do too.
One template per post — don't mix templates within a single graphic. Keep each post clearly one of the three types.
